<reason>Side A built a cleaner, more comprehensive case that stayed anchored to the proposition while systematically neutralizing Side B's objections. Side A successfully showed that Side B was conflating an unfunded status quo with supported home care, and exposed Side B's faulty economic premise that home care requires 24/7 one-on-one staffing for seniors who only need a few hours of daily help. When Side B argued that progressive decline justifies early institutional placement, Side A effectively answered the "delayed transition" concern by explaining how visiting professionals spot decline early, while framing Side B's model as premature institutionalization that strips capable seniors of autonomy years too soon.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's pressure questions ([A3.1]-[A3.2]) and subsequent follow-up in [A4.1]-[A4.3] and [A5.1]-[A5.3]: Side A forced Side B to admit to advocating "early facility placement" before 24/7 care is needed ([B4.3]), while simultaneously showing that regular visits from home aides provide the exact clinical oversight needed to trigger timely transitions before a crisis hits.</best_rebuttal>
